summary: This document updates the definitions of IPv6 multicast scopes, which determine how far a multicast packet may travel. It updates RFCs 4007 and 4291.

eli5.summary: Shouting in a room reaches a different crowd than shouting across a stadium. This RFC adjusts the list of how far a group message may travel in IPv6.

questions: how far does ipv6 multicast go
subtitle: Gives IPv6 multicast scope value 3 a real meaning: Realm-Local, a scope found automatically from the network.

tldr.problem: RFC 4291 marked multicast scope value 3 as reserved, but a multicast protocol for mesh networks wanted to use it for a scope that is wider than Link-Local yet worked out automatically. RFC 4007 and RFC 4291 also disagreed on how scope 3 is configured.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7346 renames scop 3 as Realm-Local, rewrites the text on which scope boundaries are automatic and which are set by administrators, and lets each network technology define its own Realm-Local scope in its own RFC.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7346 updates RFC 4291 and RFC 4007. It defines Realm-Local for IEEE 802.15.4 networks and creates an IANA registry of multicast scopes.

facts.label: IEEE 802.15.4 Realm-Local
facts.value: All interfaces sharing a PAN ID

today: RFC 7346 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2014. It updates RFC 4007 and RFC 4291, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Scope 3 Needed a Definition
sections.content:
RFC 4291 defines scop as a 4-bit multicast scope value used to limit the scope of a multicast group. It defines scop 3 as reserved.

The multicast protocol specification called MPL wanted to use scop 3 to carry multicast traffic scoped to a network of nodes connected in a mesh. That needs a scope greater than Link-Local whose boundary is still found automatically from the network architecture.
sections.eli5: The list of message-reach sizes had a blank spot. A new kind of network needed a size between 'just this wire' and 'a whole site', so someone had to fill it in.

sections.title: The Updated Scope Table
sections.content:
The RFC replaces the scope table of RFC 4291. Scop 3 is now Realm-Local scope. The assigned values are 1 Interface-Local, 2 Link-Local, 3 Realm-Local, 4 Admin-Local, 5 Site-Local, 8 Organization-Local and E Global. Values 0 and F stay reserved. Values 6, 7, 9, A, B, C and D are unassigned.

The RFC also rewrites the part of Section 2.7 of RFC 4291 about Admin-Local scope. Interface-Local, Link-Local and Realm-Local boundaries are automatically derived from physical connectivity or other non-multicast-related configuration. Global scope has no boundary. The boundaries of all other non-reserved scopes of Admin-Local or larger are administratively configured.
sections.eli5: Some reach sizes are set by the shape of the network itself, like a room's walls. Others are drawn by a person, like a fence. This RFC says which is which.

sections.title: How Realm-Local Scopes Work
sections.content:
Under RFC 4007, the zone of a Realm-Local scope must fall within zones of larger scope. Because Realm-Local zones are configured automatically while larger zones are configured manually, administrators must take care that this inclusion constraint is met.

Realm-Local scopes created by different network technologies are independent and have different zone indices. A router with interfaces on links using different network technologies does not forward traffic between the Realm-Local multicast scopes defined by those technologies.

The definition of any Realm-Local scope for a particular network technology should be published in an RFC, for example an 'IPv6-over-foo' RFC. That RFC must ask IANA to list it under the Realm-Local entry.
sections.eli5: Each kind of network gets its own 'neighborhood' for scope 3, and neighborhoods of different kinds do not pass messages to each other. Each kind must write down its own rules.

sections.title: Fixing RFC 4007 and the 802.15.4 Definition
sections.content:
RFC 4007 (Section 5) and RFC 4291 (Section 2.7) disagreed on how scop 3 is configured. To resolve that, the last bullet in Section 5 of RFC 4007 is replaced. The old text said zone boundaries for scopes other than interface-local, link-local and global must be defined and configured by network administrators. The new text says boundaries are defined by the IPv6 addressing architecture and updated by RFC 7346.

The RFC also gives the first Realm-Local definition. In an IP-over-IEEE802.15.4 network, scop 3 includes all interfaces sharing a Personal Area Network Identifier (PAN ID).
sections.eli5: Two rule books said different things about who draws the line for scope 3. This RFC fixes one of them so they agree. It also says that in tiny wireless networks, the neighborhood is everyone with the same network name tag.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Security
sections.content:
IANA has created an "IPv6 Multicast Address Scopes" sub-registry inside the "IPv6 Multicast Address Space Registry", filled with the table above. New scope definitions follow the "IETF Review" policy. Each future RFC defining a Realm-Local scope for a new network technology gets a reference added under scop 3, and must explicitly ask for it.

On security, the RFC says it has no security considerations beyond those in RFC 4007 and RFC 4291.
sections.eli5: A public notebook lists every reach size. When a new network type defines its neighborhood, it gets written in the notebook. The RFC adds no new safety worries.
